questions.stem: Where does the chapter say SLED lifecycle management actually breaks down?
choices: The Joiner phase, because new-hire tickets are usually incomplete
The Leaver phase, because terminations rarely generate a ticket
The Mover phase, because a role change updates HR and often never opens an IT ticket
All three phases equally, because each one depends on a manual ticket
questions.explanation: Joiner and Leaver events are discrete and visible. A role change updates the HR record and frequently generates no IT action, so the new access is added and the old access stays.

questions.stem: On a Mover event, what does a SailPoint Role do that most IAM tools do not?
choices: Provisions the new role's access and removes the access tied to the role the person left
Provisions the new access and leaves the old entitlements for the next certification
Opens a ticket so a manager can decide which old access to keep
Suspends the identity until IT confirms the transfer in the HR system
questions.explanation: The chapter's proof point is the asymmetry: most tools can grant new access on a job change, and very few automatically remove the old access. That removal is what stops privilege creep.

questions.stem: What do Lifecycle States govern, as distinct from Roles?
choices: The individual entitlements inside one business function
The overall status of the identity, such as leave of absence or termination
Peer-group recommendations during an access certification
Nested Active Directory group membership for a single application
questions.explanation: Roles handle granular access by business function. Lifecycle States handle broader status changes, such as Terminated or Leave of Absence, and trigger global provisioning policy.

questions.stem: A prospect says HR already notifies IT when someone leaves. What is the chapter's response?
choices: Agree and move on, because terminations are the Mover problem
Redirect from terminations to the role changes that update HR and never open a ticket
Offer a faster ticket so those HR emails become ServiceNow tasks
Explain that SailPoint replaces HR as the system that records terminations
questions.explanation: Terminations are the easy, visible case. Privilege accumulates on the hundreds of mid-lifecycle role changes that produce an HR record and no IT ticket.

questions.stem: The prospect runs PeopleSoft and assumes SailPoint cannot connect. What do you say?
choices: PeopleSoft is unsupported, so they need to move HR to Workday first
Banner is covered, but PeopleSoft always requires a custom build before a demo
PeopleSoft is well covered in the SLED base; confirm the specific system before going further
Any HR system connects the same day through a generic file drop
questions.explanation: The chapter treats Banner and PeopleSoft as common, covered systems. A custom HR system with no API is the case that changes the automation story, so qualify the platform in discovery.

questions.stem: Why does the chapter tell you to keep Roles and Lifecycle States separate when you explain them?
choices: Roles govern access per business function, and Lifecycle States govern overall identity status
They are the same feature under two names, and blending them shortens the pitch
Lifecycle States replace Roles once the HR feed is live
Roles apply only in higher education and Lifecycle States only in state agencies
questions.explanation: Blending the two confuses the buyer. Roles recalculate access for a business function. Lifecycle States change the identity's overall status, such as leave or termination.

questions.stem: How does the chapter say auditors read a certification with a 99% approval rate?
choices: As proof that access is appropriate
As evidence the control did not actually function
As a sign the Role model is complete
As the target outcome of the AI recommendations
questions.explanation: Managers facing hundreds of cryptic entitlements approve everything. A near-100% approval rate documents a control that did not work, which auditors increasingly write up.

questions.stem: After Role-based certification, what decision is the manager left with?
choices: Certifying each AD group the employee holds
Validating every entitlement stored inside the Role
Whether this person still needs to be in that business Role
Setting the peer-group threshold the AI will use
questions.explanation: The Role Owner already validates the entitlements inside the Role. The manager's review collapses to one question, which is how a 45-row review becomes a one-row review.

questions.stem: Who certifies that the entitlements inside a Role are still correct?
choices: The employee's manager, during the regular campaign
The Role Owner, in a separate and more expert review
The auditor, as part of the NIST exam
The Access Intelligence Center, with no human review
questions.explanation: Role certification and manager certification are different reviews. The Role Owner checks the contents. The manager checks whether the person still belongs in the Role.

questions.stem: What peer-group threshold does the chapter document for AI recommendations?
choices: Recommend approval when more than half of peers hold the access
Recommend approval above 70% of the peer group, and revocation at 70% or below
Recommend revocation unless the manager certified the same access last quarter
Recommend approval only when every peer holds the same access
questions.explanation: Above 70% the system recommends approval. At 70% or below it recommends revocation. The documented number gives an auditor a defensible rationale for each decision.

questions.stem: What does the Access Intelligence Center change about audit preparation?
choices: It builds the full Role model automatically
It turns evidence gathering from a staffing project into a report you run
It routes high-risk access requests to a quorum
It discovers unsanctioned SaaS applications
questions.explanation: AIC is the audit command center. It produces real-time, export-ready evidence without IT building custom reports.

questions.stem: A prospect says they already run access reviews every quarter. What do you ask next?
choices: What the approval rate is, because a rate above 95% means the review runs but does not function
Whether they can move to monthly reviews so auditors see more campaigns
Which SIEM they use to store the review exports
Why quarterly reviews are out of line with NIST
questions.explanation: The value is not reviewing more often. If the approval rate is above 95%, the campaign is completing without producing real decisions.

questions.stem: A prospect says their SIEM already provides this visibility. What distinction does the chapter draw?
choices: A SIEM shows what happened; Identity Graph shows what the identity is entitled to reach if it has not acted yet
A SIEM and Identity Graph answer the same question with a different picture
Identity Graph replaces the SIEM for log correlation
A SIEM already includes blast radius for service accounts and agents
questions.explanation: The SIEM reports events that fired. Identity Graph answers what a compromised identity can reach before it acts, which is the containment decision.

questions.stem: Which Identity Graph capability produces point-in-time evidence for an audit?
choices: Comparison Mode
Outlier heatmaps
Snapshots
Access path tracing
questions.explanation: A Snapshot saves an identity's relationships, entitlements, and risk signals and can be exported as JSON or CSV. Blast radius sells the incident. Snapshots sell the recurring audit need.

questions.stem: What does the chapter treat as the differentiator against other access visualizations?
choices: Color-coded rings that highlight peer differences
Showing AI agents, service accounts, and machine identities in the same graph as users
A faster CSV export than a typical SIEM
A map limited to human user entitlements
questions.explanation: Competitors can show user access maps. Non-human coverage in the same graph is what they cannot match, so the chapter says not to present this as human-only visibility.

questions.stem: What is Comparison Mode for?
choices: Placing two identities side by side to spot over-provisioning and peer deviations
Saving a point-in-time graph an auditor can export
Automatically revoking every outlier entitlement
Replacing SIEM correlation rules
questions.explanation: Comparison Mode uses a color-coded split view. Rings turn orange or red where two identities differ, which fits a promotion review or an outlier alert.

questions.stem: How does the chapter say you should open an Identity Graph demo?
choices: Open the visual first so the buyer sees the product immediately
Frame a live incident, such as a Friday credential leak, and then show the graph
Start on the DAS file-share nodes before any scenario
Lead with the JSON export format auditors will receive
questions.explanation: Without an investigation, the graph looks like a diagram. The Friday-afternoon credential leak makes the picture answer a containment decision under time pressure.

questions.stem: What does Data Access Security integration add inside the graph?
choices: Application entitlements only
Sensitive file repositories and data stores the identity can reach, in the same blast-radius view
DLP alerts for data in motion
Password hashes for the compromised account
questions.explanation: DAS applications and resources appear as nodes, so one compromised identity shows both application access and unstructured data it can reach.

questions.stem: How do static approval chains fail, according to the chapter?
choices: Only by making low-risk requests too slow
Only by giving high-risk requests too little review
In both directions: too slow for low risk and too shallow for high risk
Only when the request starts in ServiceNow
questions.explanation: One path for every request creates maximum friction and minimum control at the same time. Safe requests wait for weeks, and sensitive requests get the same cursory review.

questions.stem: Which three routing modes does the chapter say you need to know?
choices: Single, serial Multi-Step, and Quorum
Manager, Role Owner, and Auditor
Auto, Ticket, and Deny
Slack, Teams, and ServiceNow
questions.explanation: Low-sensitivity requests can take a single approver or auto-approval. High-sensitivity requests take a serial chain or a quorum where a defined majority must sign off.

questions.stem: A security buyer objects to auto-approval. What is the reframe?
choices: Auto-approval is blanket, so it should be kept out of SLED deployments
Access that matches a known peer baseline can be a stronger control than a context-free manual approval
Auto-approval is only used for terminations
The buyer is right, and every request should keep a human approver
questions.explanation: It is a policy decision, not a blanket bypass. Scrutiny moves to the sensitive requests. A single approver with no context is often the weaker control.

questions.stem: How should you position SailPoint when the customer already uses ServiceNow for requests?
choices: Replace ServiceNow so users request access inside SailPoint
Keep ServiceNow as the front door and add identity-context routing behind the ticket
Leave routing in ServiceNow, because it already evaluates identity context
Avoid mentioning ServiceNow so the conversation stays on SailPoint
questions.explanation: Many SLED accounts have a ServiceNow investment. SailPoint integrates rather than replaces it. ServiceNow routes a configured path. SailPoint decides the path from identity context.

questions.stem: Why does the Generic Approval Policy matter to an auditor?
choices: It applies only to application access requests
One engine covers role changes, exceptions, and custom workflows, so there is one audit trail
It replaces the need for a Role model
It is a plugin that lives entirely inside ServiceNow
questions.explanation: The same Single, Multi-Step, and Quorum logic applies beyond access requests. Auditors get one consistent trail for governance actions instead of several partial ones.

questions.stem: A student worker requests financial aid database access. Where should that request route?
choices: Auto-approval, because students need access the same day
A quorum or a serial chain through manager, data owner, and security
The same single approver used for standard campus software
A helpdesk ticket that carries no identity context
questions.explanation: The chapter uses that request as the high-sensitivity path. Any denial ends it. The low-risk contrast is a professor requesting standard campus software.

questions.stem: What does the chapter say about machine identities in a typical environment?
choices: They are rare, and each one already has a named owner
They outnumber human identities, and most have no designated owner
They are covered automatically once human joiner-mover-leaver is automated
They only exist in cloud accounts, not in Active Directory
questions.explanation: The pitch states that service accounts and bots often outnumber people ten to one in SLED agencies and carry significant privilege without a real owner.

questions.stem: What is an Application Identity in this chapter?
choices: The password for a single service account
A grouping that turns many disconnected accounts for one system into one reviewable business unit
The human who administers Active Directory
A spreadsheet of vendor technical contacts
questions.explanation: Application Identities are the key concept. Reviewers certify a business unit instead of dozens of disconnected accounts that happen to support the same system.

questions.stem: Which capability does the chapter call the differentiator competitors struggle to match?
choices: Discovery of service accounts, which several vendors already claim
Enforced ownership with automated succession when the owner leaves
A one-time count of how many service accounts exist
Vaulting the service account password
questions.explanation: Discovery is table stakes. Succession is the root-cause control: when the owner departs, the account is reassigned instead of becoming an orphan.

questions.stem: What happens in SailPoint when the primary owner of a machine identity leaves?
choices: The account is deleted the same day, even if a workload still depends on it
Ownership is reassigned so the account does not become orphaned
The account stays as-is until someone updates a spreadsheet
The account is excluded from certification until a new owner volunteers
questions.explanation: Ownership succession is the point of the chapter. Departure reassigns the account rather than leaving it with no one accountable.

questions.stem: What discovery question does the chapter say lands harder than a vendor breach statistic?
choices: How many service accounts exist in Active Directory today?
What is your SIEM's log retention period?
How many Roles have you finished modeling?
What was your last certification approval rate?
questions.explanation: Most prospects cannot answer the count. SLED buyers are saturated with breach numbers, and a gap in their own environment is the stronger opener.

questions.stem: A prospect says their service accounts are documented in a spreadsheet. How do you respond?
choices: Treat the spreadsheet as sufficient if it is reviewed once a year
Note that project-created accounts usually never make it back onto the list, so the real count is higher
Import the spreadsheet and stop discovery there
Explain that spreadsheets are the right system of record for machine ownership
questions.explanation: The spreadsheet is usually accurate for accounts someone remembered. Discovery almost always finds more, because accounts created during projects were never written down.

questions.stem: Why does an AI agent need a named human owner?
choices: An agent cannot be accountable for itself
Agents are not identities and cannot hold access
The CIO must personally approve every prompt the agent sends
Ownership can wait until the agent leaves pilot
questions.explanation: Agents act as privileged identities. Human accountability, with succession when that person leaves, is the governance mechanism because the agent cannot own its own access.

questions.stem: Which caveat about agent discovery does the chapter say you must state accurately?
choices: Agent discovery is not available for Microsoft Foundry Classic
Copilot Studio agents cannot be discovered or registered
Amazon Bedrock requires a separate SailPoint tenant
ServiceNow agents can only be added by a manual spreadsheet
questions.explanation: Discovery covers platforms including Bedrock, Copilot Studio, Agentforce, ServiceNow, and Vertex AI, or manual registration. Foundry Classic is the exception, so qualify the deployment type first.

questions.stem: How does this chapter differ from Chapter 16, Agentic Fabric?
choices: They describe the same product and can be used interchangeably
This chapter governs agents as identities inside ISC; Agentic Fabric discovers agents and other non-human identities, including shadow AI, across the enterprise
This chapter is shadow AI, and Agentic Fabric is limited to human access reviews
Agentic Fabric replaces agent governance inside ISC
questions.explanation: The chapter warns against conflating them. Chapter 7 is agent identity governance in ISC. Chapter 16 is enterprise discovery of agents and non-human identities, including shadow AI.

questions.stem: A prospect says their AI is still a pilot and they will govern it later. What is the response?
choices: Agree, because a pilot has no production credentials
Test it: pilots usually run on real data, so access that can read production data is production risk now
Exclude pilots from identity governance until a Chief AI Officer is named
Wait until the agent is procured through central IT
questions.explanation: The pilot label describes business commitment, not access. If the agent can read production data today, governing it now is cheaper than retrofitting it after it is embedded.

questions.stem: What happens in SailPoint when an AI agent's human owner leaves?
choices: The agent is deleted automatically
Accountability is reassigned through succession instead of being left with no owner
The agent keeps the departed person's permissions with no further review
IT opens a ticket at the next quarterly certification
questions.explanation: Succession is the same core mechanism as machine-identity ownership. The agent stays governed by a living person rather than inheriting a vacancy.

questions.stem: Which artifact does the chapter tell you to reference in discovery?
choices: The Identities Overpermissioned by Agents report
The Access Intelligence Center Role catalog
The Password Intercept log
The Role Owner spreadsheet
questions.explanation: The report is a concrete thing to ask about: which identities an agent can reach beyond what those people should have.

questions.stem: How does the chapter describe when a SailPoint workflow runs?
choices: As a nightly batch of joiner tickets
When an event occurs, such as an HR change, a risk signal, a discovered account, or a completed certification
Only after an administrator exports a report
Only when someone requests a password reset
questions.explanation: Workflows are event-driven. Those triggers start automation in real time rather than waiting for a person to run a script.

questions.stem: Why does the External/HTTP trigger matter in a SLED environment?
choices: Every legacy system needs custom code written inside SailPoint
Any legacy system can start a governed workflow through REST without SailPoint-side development
It only works when the HR system is Workday
It replaces the visual builder for process owners
questions.explanation: SLED estates include systems SailPoint will not have a native project for. The HTTP trigger lets those systems start a governed workflow through REST.

questions.stem: Why does the chapter say a failing script is more dangerous than a slow manual process?
choices: Scripts on the security path fail silently, and often only one person can change them
Scripts are always faster, so the only risk is license cost
Manual processes have an audit trail and scripts never do
Scripts cannot open an ITSM ticket
questions.explanation: The objection response is that the question is what happens when the script fails, and who else can modify it. Silent failure plus a single maintainer is the risk.

questions.stem: Who can build and maintain workflows, according to the chapter?
choices: Only developers
Process owners, because the builder is visual
External auditors during the annual review
The HRIS vendor's professional services team
questions.explanation: The visual builder is the answer to 'we do not have staff to build workflows.' Process owners can maintain the automation instead of depending on one script author.

questions.stem: How should you position Workflows relative to the rest of the platform?
choices: As a standalone product competing with the ITSM suite
As the orchestration layer underneath other capabilities, not a separate tool
As a replacement for the SIEM
As a password vault for emergency offboarding
questions.explanation: The chapter says Workflows is the engine under several other capabilities. Selling it as a standalone tool undersells that role.

questions.stem: Which action does the chapter give as an example of a workflow that is not just provisioning?
choices: Opening an ITSM ticket during a process such as emergency offboarding
Replacing the customer's SIEM correlation rules
Editing the HR system of record directly
Issuing a physical PIV card
questions.explanation: The elevator pitch names emergency offboarding and opening ITSM tickets as the work the engine takes off the team, with every action logged.

questions.stem: Why are non-employees structurally ungoverned in most SLED organizations?
choices: They use weaker passwords than employees
No authoritative HR source exists for them
They are excluded from Active Directory by policy
Sponsors are not allowed to approve access
questions.explanation: Employees have an HR feed. Contractors, vendors, and visiting personnel do not, so nothing authoritative tells identity what they should have or when they should lose it.

questions.stem: Where does the chapter say the non-employee process usually fails?
choices: Onboarding, because nobody requests the account
Offboarding, because nothing forces the department to tell IT when the work ends
Both phases equally, because contractors skip MFA
Only when the NERM add-on has not been purchased
questions.explanation: Someone has to request an account before the contractor can start, so onboarding usually happens. When the engagement ends, the department has no reason to contact IT.

questions.stem: What do you lead with, and what requires the add-on?
choices: Lead with the NERM add-on, because baseline lifecycle is not in ISC
Lead with baseline Non-Employee Lifecycle Management in ISC; NERM is the enterprise-scale add-on
Neither is in ISC; both are separate products
NERM is included, and the baseline lifecycle is the paid add-on
questions.explanation: The chapter is explicit: baseline sponsor-driven lifecycle is included. NERM is for large contractor populations that need enterprise-scale risk scoring and more complex approvals.

questions.stem: Why does the sponsor model fix offboarding better than an IT-owned process?
choices: IT knows the contract end date because IT provisioned the account
The department that engaged the contractor is the one that knows when the work ends
The vendor's own HR system becomes the source of truth
Sponsors only approve the initial request and then IT takes over
questions.explanation: Accountability has to sit with the people who know the engagement is over. IT learns too late, or never, if the process depends on that department remembering to call.

questions.stem: Beyond orphaned access, what risk do shared guest accounts create?
choices: They are an efficient pattern the chapter recommends
They break attribution, which is its own audit finding
They are required for FERPA research access
They are the same problem as employee privilege creep
questions.explanation: A shared guest account means you cannot say who acted. That is a distinct finding from an account that simply outlived its contract.

questions.stem: A prospect says contractors already follow the same onboarding as employees. What do you say?
choices: Agree, and treat non-employee governance as solved
Onboarding is the part that works; offboarding breaks because nothing forces the conversation when the contract ends
Contractors should never share any step with employee onboarding
Require every contractor to be hired into Workday before the conversation continues
questions.explanation: The account has to be requested before work starts. Nothing forces a notification when the work stops, so the test is whether ended contracts have disabled accounts.

questions.stem: How do you distinguish Data Access Security from DLP?
choices: They are the same control with different packaging
DLP watches data in motion; DAS governs who should have access in the first place
DAS replaces an incumbent DLP product
DLP classifies permissions, and DAS blocks outbound email
questions.explanation: If the buyer hears a DLP replacement, you get compared to an incumbent you should not try to displace. Broad permissions are also why DLP throws so many alerts.

questions.stem: Why does unstructured data sit outside ordinary application IAM?
choices: A large share of sensitive SLED data lives in files and shares that application entitlements never see
Unstructured data is already covered once Roles are modeled
Only databases hold sensitive agency or student data
File shares are out of scope for SLED audits
questions.explanation: The chapter's premise is that breaches involve over-privileged access to files and shared folders. Application-level IAM has no view of that effective permission.

questions.stem: Why does nested group inheritance make a manual file-permission review impractical?
choices: Effective access is inherited through groups, so a folder listing hides who can really reach the data
Nested groups reduce every review to a single business Role
DAS ignores nested groups and only reads direct ACLs
Nested groups exist only in cloud SharePoint, not on file servers
questions.explanation: DAS maps effective permissions, including nested groups, back to an identity. A person reading the folder ACL cannot see that chain.

questions.stem: What do data owner certifications apply to?
choices: The same review discipline used for application entitlements, pointed at folders and repositories
Manager certifications, which they replace
An optional review the chapter says to skip
Database tables only
questions.explanation: Owners of the repositories review access the way application owners review entitlements, instead of leaving file shares with no certification.

questions.stem: How should you position DAS against a standalone DSPM tool?
choices: Call it a generic DSPM product with no identity context
Use the DSPM category so the problem is familiar, then differentiate on native ISC integration and remediation
Never mention DSPM, because the category is unrelated
Concede that DSPM already remediates access through SailPoint Roles
questions.explanation: The chapter says to use the DSPM frame for familiarity and then show what a standalone tool does not have: the identity platform and a path to fix the permission.

questions.stem: What does DAS integration with Identity Graph give you that either view alone does not?
choices: A blast radius that spans application access and unstructured data in one picture
A replacement for DLP alerting
Password hashes for every account that touched a file share
A separate graph that excludes human users
questions.explanation: The chapter calls the unified blast radius the differentiator. Selling DAS without it leaves the strongest point out of the conversation.

questions.stem: Why does vaulting a credential fail to remove standing privilege?
choices: A person still checks the credential out and holds it to perform the routine task
Vaults cannot rotate passwords
Standing privilege is only a problem for accounts that were never vaulted
Privileged Task Automation is meant to replace the vault entirely
questions.explanation: Vaulting secures and audits the secret. The technician still possesses it for the task. PTA runs the task so the person never sees the credential.

questions.stem: Who executes the privileged task, and what does the technician see?
choices: The technician copies the password and runs the task from their own session
The Privileged Action Gateway runs it, and the technician never sees the credential
The PAM session recorder runs it after the technician reads the password
A script on a file share runs it using a shared Domain Admin password
questions.explanation: The path is a workflow with hidden credentials, a Launcher entitlement, Launchpad delegation, and execution through the Privileged Action Gateway.

questions.stem: What Parameter Storage limitation must you state before a federal-tier conversation?
choices: It is available in every AWS region, including GovCloud
It is limited to AWS us-east-1 and us-west-2 and is not available in FedRAMP GovCloud
It runs only on Azure
It requires an on-premises vault
questions.explanation: The chapter flags this as a hard limitation to say proactively. It disqualifies prospects who need the capability inside FedRAMP GovCloud.

questions.stem: How do you position PTA when the customer already has a PAM tool?
choices: PTA replaces PAM, so the vault can be retired
PAM secures the credential for discretionary admin work; PTA removes the need to hold it for routine tasks, and most customers run both
PAM is obsolete for SLED agencies
PTA only resets end-user passwords
questions.explanation: They are adjacent. Attacking the incumbent PAM program starts a fight the chapter tells you not to have.

questions.stem: Why does the Launcher Entitlement matter after the task is delegated?
choices: It is hidden from governance so technicians are not slowed down
It is governed like any other access, so the delegation can be certified and revoked
It is a policy inside the PAM vault, outside SailPoint
It grants permanent Domain Admin to the helpdesk
questions.explanation: Delegation itself has to be governed. Otherwise the scripted approach leaves an access path that certification never sees.

questions.stem: What does the technician actually do in the Launchpad?
choices: Checks an admin password out of the vault and uses it
Fills out a form, and the job runs while the credential stays hidden
Waits for a domain admin to perform the task
Uses their own standing administrative rights
questions.explanation: The helpdesk keeps the capability. Standing privilege for that routine task goes away because the credential never reaches the technician.

questions.stem: What name does the chapter say to use in front of a customer?
choices: SAAM
SailPoint Application Onboarding
Application Identity Security
Shadow IT Center
questions.explanation: SAAM is retired branding. Using it makes the capability sound like a product the customer may have already evaluated under an old name.

questions.stem: What does the guided onboarding flow deliver quickly, and what does it not?
choices: Deep entitlement governance for every complex application, in a few days
Baseline governance quickly; deep entitlement governance for complex applications still takes longer
A spreadsheet of application names and nothing else
Automatic decommission of every shadow IT application
questions.explanation: The chapter's precision point is the 70% reduction and 'days rather than months' for baseline governance. Promising full entitlement depth on that timeline oversells it.

questions.stem: Which two numbers quantify the governance gap?
choices: Helpdesk ticket volume and certification approval rate
How many applications exist, and how many are actually under identity governance
Employee headcount and contractor headcount
Password-reset percentage and MFA adoption
questions.explanation: The discovery questions ask both. The distance between the two numbers is the coverage gap audits eventually find.

questions.stem: A prospect says they only care about critical applications. What is the chapter's point?
choices: Tier-3 applications are acceptable risk and should stay out of scope
Attackers use the least-defended path, and a Tier-3 app often shares credentials or network position with something critical
Auditors have agreed to ignore anything below Tier 1
Tier-3 applications cannot hold credentials
questions.explanation: Prioritizing critical apps is reasonable. The objection response is that attackers and, increasingly, auditors do not stop at the customer's tier list.

questions.stem: A prospect says they evaluated SAAM before. What do you say?
choices: SAAM was cancelled and the capability no longer exists
SAAM is retired branding; the current name is SailPoint Application Onboarding
Keep calling it SAAM so their earlier evaluation still maps one-to-one
SAAM is a separate product they would buy alongside Application Onboarding
questions.explanation: The chapter's instruction is simply to use the current name. Treating SAAM as a different or cancelled product misstates what they looked at.

questions.stem: Which three capabilities does the chapter group under Application Onboarding?
choices: Continuous shadow IT discovery, risk-prioritized intelligence, and a simplified onboarding flow
Password sync, breach-list checking, and helpdesk deflection
Blast radius, Snapshots, and Comparison Mode
Sponsor onboarding, contract end dates, and guest-account attribution
questions.explanation: Discovery finds what is unsanctioned, intelligence says what to onboard first, and the guided flow brings an application under baseline governance.

questions.stem: About what share of SLED helpdesk tickets does the chapter attribute to password resets?
choices: About 10%
Around 40%
Password resets are rare in higher education
About 90% once MFA is turned on
questions.explanation: The chapter uses roughly 40% as the typical figure, then tells you to ask for their number because their own figure is the business case.

questions.stem: Why ask the prospect for their password-reset percentage instead of quoting the benchmark?
choices: Their number is required to price the module
A number they produce is more persuasive than a vendor statistic
The chapter says never to discuss ticket volume
The percentage is how you size the Role model
questions.explanation: Same pattern as the Mover-volume question. The prospect's own ticket mix makes the cost real without a vendor claim they can dismiss.

questions.stem: What compliance point does Dictionary Check support?
choices: It spell-checks the password against the user's name
It tests passwords against known breach lists, which CJIS and FISMA specifically require
It is a best practice with no named control behind it
It replaces MFA for student populations
questions.explanation: In a government conversation, tying the check to CJIS and FISMA is stronger than calling it a best practice.

questions.stem: What problem does Password Intercept solve?
choices: It forces every password change to start in SailPoint
It captures a change made in Active Directory and propagates it downstream without changing how users reset passwords
It blocks all password changes that originate in Active Directory
It synchronizes passwords only for cloud applications
questions.explanation: Users keep their current habit of changing the password in AD. Intercept picks that change up and pushes it to the other systems.

questions.stem: A prospect says they are going passwordless. What is the response?
choices: Agree and drop password management from the conversation
Passwordless arrives in phases; legacy systems still have passwords, and synchronization covers that transition
Passwordless makes synchronization unnecessary on the first day
SailPoint does not fit an environment that plans to be passwordless
questions.explanation: Modern systems move first. Mainframes and legacy applications keep passwords longer. The capability covers that gap rather than competing with the passwordless program.

questions.stem: What actually removes password fatigue across disconnected systems?
choices: Universal synchronization, so one change propagates everywhere
Giving each system its own password policy on purpose
Running synchronization only at the start of the semester
Replacing MFA with a single shared password
questions.explanation: A self-service reset on one system does not help if the user still keeps a different password everywhere else. Synchronization is the part that removes the written-down credential.

questions.stem: What is MCP, as this chapter defines it?
choices: A SailPoint protocol that replaces approval workflows
An open standard from Anthropic that lets an AI assistant connect to enterprise systems
A FedRAMP authorization package for GovCloud
A password-vault API
questions.explanation: SailPoint's MCP Server uses that open standard so an existing enterprise assistant can submit and track access requests. It is not a new approval engine.

questions.stem: Which four actions does the SailPoint MCP Server support?
choices: List requestable items, initiate a request, query status, and cancel a request
Approve, deny, escalate, and revoke
Discover agents, sanction an app, rotate a secret, and scan a repository
Reset a password, intercept a change, synchronize, and lock an account
questions.explanation: Those four are the documented actions. Approval is deliberately not one of them. The assistant initiates and tracks; the existing workflow decides.

questions.stem: A security buyer says they do not want AI making access decisions. What is the precise correction?
choices: The assistant approves low-risk requests and holds high-risk ones
The AI initiates and tracks the request; the existing approvers still decide
AI replaces quorum approvals for sensitive data
The chatbot approves the request and writes the audit record afterward
questions.explanation: The chapter says to be precise: MCP is the interface. Who approves what does not change, which is what defuses the objection.

questions.stem: What audit record does an MCP action produce?
choices: A chat transcript the user can delete
A timestamped immutable record suitable as CJIS, FERPA, and FISMA evidence
No record, because the request was conversational
A weekly email summary to the security officer
questions.explanation: Natural language is only the front end. Every action is written so an auditor can use it as evidence.

questions.stem: Which two capabilities are unavailable in FedRAMP GovCloud?
choices: Harbor Pilot and the MCP Server
Only Harbor Pilot; the MCP Server is available
MCP, if the model is hosted locally
Neither; GovCloud is the primary deployment for both
questions.explanation: The chapter calls out both. Positioning either to a federal-tier agency without checking the deployment is a credibility failure.

questions.stem: What stays the same after a user requests access through an enterprise assistant?
choices: Who approves the request
The assistant becomes an approver for low-risk items
The audit requirement is waived for chat requests
The approval chain is rewritten for natural language
questions.explanation: The objection response is that nothing about who approves what changes. The assistant is the front door, and the governed workflow is still the decision.

questions.stem: What is the Shared Signals Framework in this chapter?
choices: A SailPoint-only log format
An open standard for real-time security event exchange, using CAEP events
A replacement for the customer's SIEM
A quarterly export of certification decisions
questions.explanation: SSF is the standard. CAEP events are how a detection tool and the identity platform exchange risk in real time instead of waiting for the next scheduled evaluation.

questions.stem: What window does SSF close?
choices: The gap between a detection in seconds and the identity platform hearing about it at the next scheduled check
The gap between joiner tickets and leaver tickets
The time a password reset spends in the helpdesk queue
The months it takes to finish a Role model
questions.explanation: Security tools see the threat immediately. Identity often does not act until the next evaluation. That delay is where the chapter says attackers work.

questions.stem: Which roles can SailPoint play in an SSF exchange?
choices: Receiver only
Transmitter only
Both Receiver and Transmitter
Neither; SSF traffic is inbound email
questions.explanation: Bidirectional support is the differentiator. SailPoint can take a risk event in and send an identity-governance finding back out to the rest of the stack.

questions.stem: A buyer refuses automated revocation. What can you propose instead?
choices: Insist on revocation for every signal, or SSF is not worth deploying
A milder response on the same spectrum, such as raising risk, launching a targeted certification, or restricting access
Turn SSF off, because the only supported response is revocation
Send the signal to a spreadsheet for the next quarterly review
questions.explanation: Responses are configurable. Revocation is one end of the spectrum, not the only action, so a cautious buyer can start with restriction or a targeted review.

questions.stem: When is SSF not worth discussing yet?
choices: When the agency has fewer than 5,000 employees
When there is no detection stack producing signals to exchange
When the customer already has a SIEM
When identity governance is already in place
questions.explanation: The chapter says to qualify for security maturity. Without detections, there is nothing for SailPoint to receive or for the rest of the stack to act on.

questions.stem: A prospect says the SIEM already correlates these signals. What is the distinction?
choices: Correlation and action are the same thing
The SIEM shows an analyst that events are related; SSF lets the signal itself trigger the access change
SSF replaces the SIEM
The SIEM should be disabled once SSF is on
questions.explanation: Someone still has to decide and execute the access change after a SIEM correlation. SSF removes that human relay from the loop.

questions.stem: What does the chapter call the fastest-growing identity risk in government right now?
choices: Staff using AI tools to do their jobs, with those tools reaching data nobody has reviewed
An external attacker with no insider path
Only sanctioned copilots that central IT deployed
Faculty email forwarding rules
questions.explanation: The shadow-AI story is that productive employees adopt ChatGPT, Copilot, and Gemini. The sanctioned count the customer can recite is not the real inventory.

questions.stem: Which of these is one of Agentic Fabric's six entity types for credentials?
choices: API keys, tokens, secrets, and certificates, including where each is used and whether it rotates
Human employees and their department cost centers
Certification campaign schedules
Helpdesk password-reset tickets
questions.explanation: The registry's six types are Agents, Applications, Accounts, MCP Clients, Credentials, and Endpoints. Credentials are the secrets those non-human identities authenticate with.

questions.stem: What do you tell a university about the browser extension before they ask?
choices: It captures document content and the body of personal email
It does not separate personal from business activity; telemetry is session metadata, not content, and the first deployment can be scoped to administrative staff
It is invisible to legal and faculty review, so leave it out of the conversation
It only runs on applications the institution has already sanctioned
questions.explanation: SailPoint's documentation says the extension does not distinguish personal and business activity and tells customers to involve legal. Raising that, plus allowlists and client-side password checks, is how you avoid a campus stall.

questions.stem: How do Business Apps change certification of non-human identities?
choices: Reviewers certify the business application and drill into individual identities only where remediation is needed
Every API key is certified on its own, with no grouping
Business Apps replace human Roles
Sanction status cannot be inherited by the identities inside the app
questions.explanation: This is the same decision-reduction idea as human certifications, applied to a much larger population. Marking an app Sanctioned also marks its associated identities.

questions.stem: What does the chapter mean by machine identity debt?
choices: Employee accounts that remain after a termination
Service accounts and keys that stay behind after a vendor integration or project ends
Unpaid invoices for cloud workloads
Passwords that have not been synchronized
questions.explanation: People get deprovisioned when they leave. The service account for a finished vendor contract usually does not, and it keeps its access.

questions.stem: Which Agentic Fabric report identifies non-human identities that have not authenticated recently?
choices: Dormancy Reporting
Password Intercept
The human Role Owner campaign
Harbor Pilot
questions.explanation: Dormancy Reporting supports least-privilege evidence by finding identities that have not authenticated in a defined window. Entitlement History, credential rotation, shadow AI, and certification records are the other audit outputs named in the chapter.

questions.stem: How should you position Entro against a vault the customer already runs?
choices: Entro replaces the vault
The vault governs secrets that made it in; Entro finds the credentials that never did
A vault already scans git history and chat tools
Entro is a linter that developers run before commit
questions.explanation: Positioning Entro as a vault replacement starts a switching-cost fight. Vaults were not built to find the key hardcoded during troubleshooting or pasted into Slack.

questions.stem: Why is deleting a secret from a repository not the same as removing it?
choices: Deleting the file deletes it from git history as well
A credential that was committed and later deleted remains in commit history
Pipeline scanners always read the full history, so this case is already covered
Commit history is out of scope for secrets scanning
questions.explanation: The chapter calls this the most persuasive technical fact in the conversation. Many buyers have never heard that git history keeps a deleted file, so the exposure is structural rather than careless.

questions.stem: How do Entro and Agentic Fabric fit together?
choices: They overlap, so the customer picks one
Agentic Fabric governs the non-human identities; Entro governs the credentials those identities use and detects misuse
Entro discovers AI agents, and Agentic Fabric scans repositories
Agentic Fabric scans Slack and email for secrets
questions.explanation: They stack. One tells you the identity exists and should be governed. The other tells you the key it uses is sitting in a repository or pipeline.

questions.stem: A team already runs a secrets scanner in the pipeline. What is still missing?
choices: Nothing, because a finding report is the whole job
Full history, plus what the credential unlocks, who owns it, and which finding to fix first
The scanner should be removed before Entro is installed
Pipeline scanners already rotate every secret they find
questions.explanation: Keep the pipeline scanner. Most of them see current state rather than history, and a list of findings without ownership and blast radius is not actionable for a small team.

questions.stem: Who does the chapter say you should enter the deal through?
choices: The developer who will feel the workflow friction
Security and compliance, with development as the implementation partner
The helpdesk, because exposed secrets become password tickets
Procurement, as a vault replacement
questions.explanation: Developers often experience the product as friction. The security buyer sees a risk register and audit evidence. Enter there, then bring development in to remediate.

questions.stem: What does the Secrets Graph add beyond a list of exposed credentials?
choices: Relationships among secrets, identities, and resources, including attack paths a single finding hides
A password-strength score for each human user
A replacement for access certifications
A catalog of the 700 secret types and nothing else
questions.explanation: Detection breadth does not make an executive act. The graph shows how one exposed credential connects to identities and systems, which is the risk story.

questions.stem: Which four populations does the master narrative say identity now includes?
choices: Employees, students, contractors, and alumni
Humans, machine identities, AI agents, and the credentials underneath them
Roles, Lifecycle States, certifications, and workflows
The SIEM, PAM, DLP, and the ITSM suite
questions.explanation: The narrative's claim is that most organizations govern people and do not govern the other three. The gaps between those populations are where breaches and audit findings land.

questions.stem: What is Movement 1 for, and what happens if you skip it?
choices: It criticizes the incumbent so the executive feels urgency
It credits the program they already built, which is what keeps them listening
It pitches all four products before the executive can object
It is optional whenever an identity vendor is already installed
questions.explanation: Executives who feel dismissed in the first minute stop listening. Movement 1 exists to recognize the human-identity program before you talk about what it does not cover.

questions.stem: What single question is the whole narrative designed to earn?
choices: Which SailPoint product should we buy today?
Which of these populations worries you most?
Can we replace your identity vendor this quarter?
How many modules are in the platform bundle?
questions.explanation: You earn the question and then stop talking. Their answer picks the next chapters more accurately than a qualification script, and filling the silence turns it back into a pitch.

questions.stem: Why does the chapter say not to pitch all four solutions in the first meeting?
choices: The story earns the question, and the question narrows the deal
The executive expects a demo of every chapter
Movement 4 is the commercial close
SLED buyers will only fund one population in total
questions.explanation: Pitching everything converts the narrative into a monologue. The deal starts with the population they name, on a platform that can cover the others later.

questions.stem: A CIO says they already have an identity vendor. What do you do instead of counter-pitching?
choices: Explain why that vendor should be replaced
Use the four populations to talk about what their current program does not cover
End the meeting, because an incumbent means there is no deal
Lead with price against the installed product
questions.explanation: The frame expands into uncovered territory without forcing a rip-and-replace fight. Most SLED accounts have an incumbent, and Movement 1 already credited that program.

questions.stem: The executive says this is too much and asks where to start. What do you propose?
choices: Walk through the other three populations anyway
A 90-day proof on the population they named, and leave the rest alone for now
A three-year transformation across all four populations
Drop the platform point and sell a single point tool
questions.explanation: That reaction is the one the narrative wants. Scope the proof to their answer. The strategic point is that the proof sits on a platform that can cover the rest when they are ready.
